segments.text: Prints one csv field: a comma and then the number `v`. For a negative `v` it prints `,NA`. The functions `read_smaps` (line 1515) and `read_vmstat` (line 1545) store -1 for a value that they did not find. So such a value appears as `NA` in a P row.
segments.heading: Function `print_na`: one csv field, or `NA`

segments.text: Prints one P row: the page state of one buffer at one reading. In the test `main` calls it at line 3117, once per buffer after each page-state reading. `pg` holds the two page values of the buffer. `vm` holds the four vmstat counters.
segments.heading: Function `print_p`: prints one P row

segments.text: Columns 1 to 5: the letter `P`, the round, the position, the thread number and the buffer letter. The position is -1 in the rows of the reading before the first interval. In all other rows it is the position of the interval that has just ended. In the test the buffer letter is always `a` [Ref5].

Columns 6 and 7, `kB_total` and `kB_huge`: the size of the mapping of the buffer, and the part of it that lies on 2 MiB pages. The unit is kB of 1024 bytes. `read_smaps` (line 1515) took both values from the Linux file smaps. In the test both are 262144 kB (256 MiB) in every P row [Ref5].

Columns 8 to 11: the four vmstat counters, in the order `thp_fault_alloc`, `thp_fault_fallback`, `thp_collapse_alloc`, `pgmigrate_success`. They count for the whole system, not for this buffer. `main` passes the same array `vm` for all buffers of one reading (line 3117). So all P rows of one reading hold the same four values.

Ends the row. Example, the first P row of the file a6456.csv in the result folder of T72L1 (the first of the 3 processes of part L): `P,0,-1,0,a,262144,262144,611480,0,2,0` [Ref5]. It says: round 0, before the first interval, thread 0, buffer `a`, a mapping of 262144 kB, 262144 kB of it on 2 MiB pages.

With `--count` each worker calls this function once (line 1644). At that moment the thread is pinned and has no buffer yet. The function opens one counter per entry of `--events`: 6 in the test [Ref4]. `t` is the record of the calling thread.
segments.heading: Function `open_counters`: opens the counter group of one thread

segments.text: Start state: no group leader (`group_fd` is -1) and 0 open counters. The group leader is the first counter of a counter group.

- One loop pass per event of `--events`.
- `a` is the structure that describes one counter to Linux.
- `memset` sets all its fields to 0. So every option that the next lines do not set is off.
- The field `disabled` also stays 0. So a counter counts from the moment it is opened.

- `type` selects the PMU: 11 in the test (`--pmu-type 11`).
- `size` gives Linux the size of the structure.
- `config` is the event code, for example 0x198 for `cbusy0` [Ref4]. The program passes the code to Linux and does not interpret it.

- `exclude_kernel = 1`: the counter does not count while the CPU runs Linux kernel code.
- `exclude_hv = 1`: it does not count hypervisor code. A hypervisor is the software that runs virtual machines.
- So the counter counts only in user mode: while the thread runs the code of the program itself.
- The specification of the first runner says that counter code without these two fields fails without root on CRB [Ref10].

`read_format` chooses what one `read` of the group returns. `PERF_FORMAT_GROUP`: the values of all counters of the group in one reading. The two other flags add the enabled time and the running time of the group [Ref8].

- The system call `perf_event_open` opens the counter. It returns a file descriptor: the number that later calls such as `read` use for the open counter. A negative value means failure.
- Arguments `0` and `-1`: the pid and the cpu argument of the call [Ref10]. Together they mean: count the calling thread, on any CPU that it runs on.
- The thread is pinned, so it runs on one CPU only.
- Argument `t->group_fd`: -1 for the first counter, which starts a new group. A later counter passes the file descriptor of the leader and joins its group.
- Last argument `0`: no flags.

- The open failed.
- Only thread 0 writes a message to stderr: the event name, the PMU type, the code and the error text.
- The event gets the position -1. `main` prints `NA` for it in the C rows (lines 3096 to 3098).
- The loop continues with the next event. The thread does not stop.
- In the test no csv field is `NA` and every stderr.txt is empty [Ref5]. So every open succeeded in all 120 threads.
The open succeeded. `ev_pos[e]` gets the position of this event in a group reading: 0 for the first open counter, 1 for the next. `nopen` counts the open counters: 6 per thread in the test.

The first counter that opens becomes the leader of the group. `group_fd` keeps its file descriptor, and every group reading uses it. The file descriptors of the other counters are not kept. The interval mode never closes, resets or stops a counter.

Returns the CPU time that the calling thread has used so far, in ns. It reads the Linux clock CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID. The worker calls it once before and once after each timed interval (lines 1686 and 1718). Both calls lie outside the timed interval.
segments.heading: Function `cpu_ns`: CPU time of the calling thread

segments.text: Takes one reading of all counters of the thread `t` and stores it in `c`. The worker calls it once before and once after each timed interval (lines 1685 and 1719). Both calls lie outside the timed interval.
segments.heading: Function `read_group`: one reading of the counter group

segments.text: Space for the largest reading: 3 header words plus 8 counter values (`MAX_EV` is 8). Each word has 8 bytes. In the test a reading has 9 words: 3 header words and 6 counter values.
A thread without an open counter returns here. Then `c` keeps the zeros that the worker wrote at line 1667.

- One `read` system call on the leader returns the whole group: the number of counters `nr`, the enabled time, the running time, then one value per counter [Ref8].
- The reading is rejected when it has fewer than 24 bytes (the 3 header words).
- It is also rejected when `nr` is not the number of counters that this thread opened.
- A rejected reading ends the whole program with a message on stderr and status 2.
- In the test every stderr.txt is empty [Ref5]. So no reading was rejected.

Stores the enabled time and the running time of the group, in ns. `main` prints the difference between the two readings of an interval as `enabled_ns` and `running_ns` in the C row (lines 3092 to 3093). In the test the two columns are equal in all 8880 C rows (checked on 2026-11-21) [Ref5]. So the counters counted during all of their enabled time.

Stores one value per open counter, in the order in which the counters were opened. `main` prints for each event the difference between the reading after the interval and the reading before it (line 3100).
The start function of every worker thread. `main` creates 120 of them at line 3012. `t` is the record of this thread: `main` has set its index `idx` and its CPU `cpu` (lines 3010 to 3011).
segments.heading: Function `worker`: one benchmark thread

segments.text: `sink` is a volatile variable on the stack of this thread. `call` stores there the sum that the old read kernel returns (line 1500). So the compiler cannot remove the adds of the old read kernel. Each thread has its own `sink`, and the threads do not store to one shared cache line.

`v` is the value that `k_write` stores into every 8-byte word of the buffer. It depends on the process number and on the thread index. The source comment gives the reason: the compiler cannot replace the store loop by `memset`. The read kernels do not use `v`.
`k` counts the timed intervals that this thread has started. Line 1677 compares it with the shared counter `gen`.

`min_ns` is the `--min-ms` value in ns: 6000000000 ns (6 s) in the test. Only the loop of `--stop pass` uses it (line 1715). The test runs with `--stop common`, so this variable does not end an interval of the test.

**CPU pinning.** The test passes `--cpus`, so `cfg.ncpus` is 120. The thread binds itself to its CPU with `pin_cpu` (line 415). Thread `i` gets CPU `i`: the threads 0 to 63 run on mesh 0, the threads 64 to 119 on mesh 1. Every later line of the worker runs on that CPU.

With `--count` the thread opens its 6 counters with `open_counters` (line 1582). The counters count from this moment on. So they also count during the first touch and the warm-up passes. A C row holds only the change between the two readings of one interval.

**Buffer allocation.** `alloc_buf` (line 434) maps buffer `a` of this thread: 268435456 bytes (256 MiB), starting at a 2 MiB boundary, with a request to Linux for 2 MiB pages. Each thread has its own buffer. A thread reads only its own buffer.

**First touch.** `k_write` (line 531) stores `v` into all 33554432 words of the buffer. The pinned thread does this write itself, before any read. Linux gives a page its physical memory at the first write. This line is not timed.
A second buffer `b` exists only with `--two-buffers` or with a copy kernel in `--seq`. The test has neither, so these lines do not run. Every P row of the test is a row of buffer `a` [Ref5].

- Two waits at the barrier. The barrier needs 121 threads: the 120 workers and the main thread (line 3005).
- First wait: all 120 buffers exist and are written. `main` arrives at line 3045. Then it copies the buffer addresses and reads the page state for the P rows with position -1.
- Second wait: the workers block until that reading is done. `main` releases them at line 3114.

The two loops over the timed intervals. `--rounds 2` runs the `--seq` list two times: round 0, then round 1. `pos` is the position in the list: 0 to 4 for like.spec, 0 to 2 for cfwd.spec and crev.spec [Ref4]. One loop pass is one interval, and `main` runs the same two loops (lines 3039 to 3040).

`kd` is the entry of the kernel table for this position: name, type and function pointer. Example: position 0 of like.spec is `oldread`, with the type T_OLDREAD and the function `k_oldread`. The order is fixed by the list. In like.spec `asmread` always runs after `oldread`, and `oldread` of round 1 runs after `read_1pl` of round 0.

`size` is the number of bytes of this position: 268435456 bytes, the whole buffer. No `--seq` entry of the test has an `@SIZE` part, so `main` has set the size to the `--bytes` value (line 2990). `nchunk` is the number of 2 MiB pieces in it: 128.
The start offset of `--start offset`. The test passes `--start common`, so `off` is 0. Every thread starts its timed interval at byte 0 of its own buffer.
A copy kernel counts every byte two times: once read, once written. The kernels of the test are read kernels, so `per_byte` is 1.

Variables of one interval. `bytes` is the byte count of the timed interval, and `p` counts its kernel calls. `sched`, `deadline`, `t0` and `t1` are clock values in ns. `r` is the result record, and `memset` sets it to zero.

**Warm-up, not timed.** One call of the kernel of this position over the whole buffer: offset 0, 268435456 bytes. So before every timed interval the thread has run the same kernel once over its whole buffer. Between this pass and the timed interval lie the barrier wait, the wait for the common start and the first counter reading (lines 1675 to 1687).
Only a process with one thread reads the page state here, in the worker. The test has 120 threads, so these lines do not run.

Barrier wait after the warm-up. The thread blocks until all 120 workers have ended their warm-up and `main` has arrived at line 3057. Then all 121 threads continue. A thread whose warm-up ends early waits here and reads no memory.

**Common start, step 1.** Lines 1676 to 1683 run only with `--stop common`, which the test uses. The thread repeats an empty loop until the shared counter `gen` equals `k + 1`. `main` adds 1 to `gen` at line 3062, after it has stored the start time and the deadline of this interval. In this loop the thread stays on its CPU and does not sleep.

Copies the common start time into `sched` and the common deadline into `deadline`. `main` computed them at lines 3059 to 3061: the start time is its clock reading plus 2 ms (`LEAD_NS`), and the deadline is the start time plus 6 s. All 120 threads read the same two values.

**Common start, step 2.** The thread reads the clock again and again until the clock reaches the start time. It leaves the loop at its first clock read at or after the start time. This spin-wait is not timed.

- With `--count`, which the test uses: the first counter reading (`read_group`), then the thread CPU time (`cpu_ns`). Both go into `r.c0`.
- These two calls run after the wait for the common start and before the clock read of line 1688.
- So they are not inside the timed interval. But `t0` is later than the common start time by at least their duration.
- In the test `t0` is 2 us to 34 us after the common start time (us = microsecond, computed on 2026-11-21 from the columns `t_sched_s` and `t_start_s` of all 8880 T rows) [Ref5]. Both columns are printed with 6 decimal places, so each time is rounded to 1 us.
**Start of the timed interval.** The thread reads the clock into `t0`. Each thread has its own `t0`. Nothing above this line is inside the timed interval.
Counts this interval. At the next interval line 1677 waits for the next value of `gen`.

The branch of `--stop common`, which the test uses. `chunk` is the number of bytes of one kernel call: 2097152 bytes (2 MiB, `CHUNK_BYTES`). `at` is the byte offset of the next chunk in the buffer. It starts at `off`, which is 0.

- **Timed kernel call.** `call` (line 1491) runs the kernel on the chunk at byte offset `at` of buffer `a`.
- The kernel gets the address of the chunk and its length in 8-byte words: 262144.
- So the kernel function is entered once per 2 MiB: 128 times per pass over the buffer.
- For `oldread`, `call` stores the returned sum in `sink` after each call. The other five kernels of the test return nothing.
- A read kernel does not get the argument `v + p++`. The `p++` only counts the calls.

- **Bytes counted.** Each finished call adds 2097152 bytes.
- This is the size of the range that was passed to the kernel. Nothing is counted inside a kernel.
- The number is the same for every read kernel. It is also used for `read_1pl`, which loads 16 B of each 64 B line.
- Example: the first T row of the file a6456.csv in the result folder of T72L1 (thread 0, `oldread`) holds 28934406144 bytes. That is 13797 calls [Ref5].

Moves `at` to the next chunk. After the last chunk of the buffer (chunk 127) the offset returns to 0. So the kernel calls go through the 256 MiB buffer from start to end and then start again at byte 0, until the interval ends.

**Clock read after every chunk.** `t1` is the clock value after this call. The last `t1` is the end of the timed interval. So the timed interval holds one clock read per 2 MiB chunk: 13797 clock reads in the example above.

- **Stop rule.** The loop repeats while `t1` is before the common deadline.
- A thread stops at its first clock read at or after the deadline. So it finishes the chunk that it is in.
- The bytes and the time of this last chunk are counted.
- The deadline is the same for all threads. Each thread has its own end time `t1`.
- In the test the last `t1` is 0 us to 463 us after the deadline [Ref5]. The elapsed time `t1 - t0` is 5.999979 s to 6.000457 s. Both ranges were computed on 2026-11-21 from all 8880 T rows, with the deadline taken as `t_sched_s` plus 6 s.
The branch of `--stop pass`. The test does not use it. Here a thread would run whole passes over its buffer and stop when its own elapsed time `t1 - t0` reaches the `--min-ms` value.

- **After the timed interval.** The interval ended at the last clock read of line 1700.
- The thread reads its thread CPU time and then takes the second counter reading. Both go into `r.c1`.
- The order is the reverse of lines 1685 to 1686. So the timed interval lies between the two CPU-time readings, and these lie between the two counter readings.
- So the counter values of a C row cover the timed interval plus a few calls around it: the two readings of the thread CPU time and the clock read `t0`.

Stores the result of this thread: the byte count, `t0` and the last `t1`. `main` computes the elapsed time of a thread as `t_end - t_start` (lines 3069 and 3082). The script stat_bwx.py computes the rate of a thread from the T row as bytes / elapsed seconds / 1e9, in GB/s [Ref6].
Stores the common start time. `main` prints it in the T row as `t_sched_s`.

**Late flag.** It is set when `t0` is more than 100000 ns (100 us, `LATE_NS`) after the common start time. `main` then prints `late` in the last column of the T row. The program does nothing else with the flag: the interval runs, and its bytes are counted. In the test no T row has the flag [Ref5].
Copies the record into the thread structure. `main` reads it there after the barrier wait of the next line.

Barrier wait at the end of the interval. The thread blocks until all 120 workers have ended their interval and `main` waits at line 3064. A thread that has stopped reads no memory while other threads finish their last chunk.

- Second barrier wait at the end of the interval.
- While the workers block here, `main` prints the I, T and C rows of the interval and reads the page state of all buffers (lines 3066 to 3113).
- `main` releases the workers at line 3114. Then each worker starts the warm-up pass of the next interval.
- `main` prints the P rows and the `# page_read` line after the release (lines 3115 to 3118). So this output can run while the workers do their warm-up.
- The output ends before the next timed interval starts. The barrier of line 1675 lets the workers pass only when `main` has finished the output and waits at line 3057.

The ends of the two loops. The worker calls no sleep function. So between two intervals lie only the waits, the readings and the warm-up pass of the rows above. After the last interval of round 1 the thread returns, and `main` waits for all threads at line 3124.

Prints the option summary to stderr and ends the program with status 2. `main` calls it for an argument that it does not accept and for settings that fail one of its checks (lines 2969 to 2995), for example `--threads` without `--cpus`. The argument lines of the test do not reach it. The text names the program `bwx`, the name of an older version of the runner.
segments.heading: Function `usage`: option summary, then exit

segments.text: `main` calls it with the text after `--seq` (line 2950). `strtok` cuts the text at every comma. Each loop pass handles one entry, in the order of the list. This order is the order in which the kernels run in each round.
segments.heading: Function `parse_seq`: reads the `--seq` list

segments.text: An entry may have the form `KERNEL@SIZE`. Then the name ends at the `@`. No entry of the test has an `@` [Ref4].
Searches the kernel table `kernels[]` (lines 1454 to 1484) for the name, from the first entry on. `k` becomes the index of the entry with this name.
A name that is not in the table ends the program with a message and status 2. So does a 65th entry (`MAX_SEQ` is 64).
Stores the index and the size of the entry in `cfg.seq`. An entry without `@SIZE` gets the size 0 here. `main` later replaces 0 by the `--bytes` value (line 2990).

- Result for like.spec: `oldread`, `asmread`, `read_nop96`, `read_nop256`, `read_1pl` (5 positions) [Ref4].
- Result for cfwd.spec: `oldread`, `read`, `asmread` (3 positions).
- Result for crev.spec: `asmread`, `read`, `oldread` (3 positions). This is the reverse order of cfwd.spec.

`main` calls it with the text after `--events` (line 2964). An entry is `NAME=CODE` or only `CODE`. The table `by_pos` holds the names for an entry without a name at one of the first 5 places of the list. Every entry of the test has a name, so the table is not used [Ref4].
segments.heading: Function `parse_events`: reads the `--events` list

segments.text: One loop pass per entry. `eq` points to the `=` sign of the entry. `code` points to the text after it.
Rejects an entry with an empty name, a 9th entry (`MAX_EV` is 8) and a name of 32 characters or more. The program then ends with a message and status 2.

Copies the text before the `=` as the name of the event. The interval mode uses the name in two places: as a column title in the header line of the C rows (line 3031), and in the error message of `open_counters` (line 1598).
Names for an entry without `=`: a name of `by_pos`, or `ev` plus the entry number. The test does not use these lines.

`strtoull` with base 0 turns the code text into a number. With base 0 a text that starts with `0x` is read as hexadecimal. A text that is not a whole number ends the program with a message and status 2.
Counts the entry. Result in the test: 6 events with the names cbusy0, cbusy1, cbusy2, cbusy3, cbusy_mt, bus_access and the codes 0x198, 0x199, 0x19a, 0x19b, 0x19c, 0x19 [Ref4].

- The trial mode starts here and ends at line 2886.
- `main` enters it only when an argument is the word `--trial` (lines 2912 to 2914). No argument line of the test holds that word [Ref4].
- So no function of this section runs in the test. The rows below say only what each part is.
- This comment describes the mode: a plan file lists the trials, a trial is a list of windows, and `timed_sequence` runs the windows.
segments.heading: Trial mode (lines 1795 to 2886): not run by the whole-chip test

segments.text: Two more headers and the constants of the trial mode. `BIN_NS` is the requested width of a bin: 10 ms. `TRACE_CAP` is the largest number of trace events per trial: 1048576. The other lines fix line 1 and line 3 of a plan file, the number of fields of a plan line (11) and upper limits for the values of a plan.

Number codes and their printed names. The first group names the four kinds of window of a trial, called phases: previous activity, prefix, predecessor and target. The second group names the states of the counters: closed, open, read and fail. The third group names the nine kinds of trace event.

`struct part` is one kernel on one buffer range for one duration in ms. `struct trial` is one line of the plan file: its text fields, the number of target windows, the counter setting, the bin setting, the duration of a target window and the four parts.

`struct bin` is one clock read of a window with the byte count at that read. `struct win` is one window. Its first group of fields is the plan: kernel, phase, index, size, passes between two clock reads, duration and bin storage. Its second group is the result: number of bins, bytes, start time and end time.

`struct trec` is the record of one trial. It holds the windows and the counter readings. It holds the page state, the thread CPU time, the context-switch counts and the page-fault counts before and after the timed sequence. It also holds the counter state, the result of the sum check (`sink_ok`) and two failure counts.

`struct tev` is one event of the trace: a clock time, a window index, the event kind and the phase. `struct tw` is the state of the worker of the trial mode. Its first field is a `struct thread`, the same record that the interval mode uses for a worker.
Three global variables of the trial mode. `plan` holds the plan file and the options of the mode. `rec` points to the records of all trials. `recsz` holds the sizes of the record storage.

Without `--trace` there is no log, and the function returns at once. Otherwise it appends one event with the time of the latest clock read. A full log (1048576 events) only raises the count of dropped events. The whole-chip test does not call this function.
segments.heading: Function `tev_add` (trial mode): adds one event to the trace

segments.text: Reads the clock with `now_ns` (line 327). With `--trace` it also stores the time and logs the read as an event. The whole-chip test does not call this function.
segments.heading: Function `tclock` (trial mode): clock read

segments.text: Reads the thread CPU time with `cpu_ns` (line 1609). With `--trace` it also logs the read as an event. The whole-chip test does not call this function.
segments.heading: Function `tcpu` (trial mode): thread CPU time

segments.text: Runs the kernel of the window `r` once on the first `r->size` bytes of the buffer. It goes through `call` (line 1491), the same function that the interval mode uses. With `--trace` it logs the first call of each window. The whole-chip test does not call this function.
segments.heading: Function `tcall` (trial mode): one kernel call of a window

segments.text: Reads the counter group and then the thread CPU time. In `read_group` (line 1617) a bad reading ends the process. Here it only adds 1 to `read_fail`. The whole-chip test does not call this function.
segments.heading: Function `tcount` (trial mode): counter reading at a window boundary

segments.text: The timed part of the trial mode. It runs the windows of one trial one after another, as the comment describes. The whole-chip test does not call this function. The timed loop of the test is in `worker` (lines 1688 to 1701).
segments.heading: Function `timed_sequence` (trial mode): the timed windows of one trial

segments.text:
- One loop pass per window.
- When the trial reads counters, a target window starts with a call of `tcount`. One more call follows after the last window.
- `t0` is the start clock read of the window.
- The inner loop runs `passes` whole passes of the kernel and then reads the clock into `t1`. It repeats until the duration of the window has passed.
- A bin closes at a clock read when its requested end has passed. It stores `t1` and the byte count.
- At the end the window record gets the bytes, `t0`, the last `t1` and the number of bins.

The same as `tcall` (line 1954), but the kernel index, the phase, the window index and the size arrive as arguments. So it reads no field of the window record. The comment `/* bwx10+ */` marks text that the version bwx10 added. The whole-chip test does not call this function.
segments.heading: Function `tcall_hot` (trial mode): `tcall` with value arguments

segments.text: The variant of `timed_sequence` that the trial-mode option `--hot-copy` selects. The whole-chip test does not call this function.
segments.heading: Function `timed_sequence_hot` (trial mode): variant for `--hot-copy`

segments.text: The same loop as lines 1997 to 2030, with one difference. Before the start clock read of a window it copies the fields of the window record into local constants (lines 2060 to 2063). It writes the results back after the end clock read (lines 2086 to 2089). The source comment says that between these two points the loop does not read or write the window record.
